title: Is that really a photo?
hook: the Gurus lived long before cameras; every picture of a Guru is an artist's work, and some online images are made up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, and your line was the word online. The screen can carry the Guru's word to the back row. Today, what else the screen carries, and how to tell. Day one thousand forty.

A message lands in a family group chat. An old, brown-tinted photograph: a man with a white beard and a gentle face, and a caption in capital letters: rare real photo of Guru Nanak. Folded hands and hearts fill the replies. An aunt forwards it to three more groups. Then a teenager types one line: cameras weren't invented until the eighteen-twenties. The chat goes very quiet. Today: is that really a photo?
screen: `A FAMILY GROUP CHAT.` → `RARE REAL PHOTO OF GURU NANAK.` → `CAMERAS CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the dates. The ten Gurus lived from 1469 to 1708. The first lasting photographs were made in the 1820s, more than a century after the tenth Guru died. So there is no photograph of any Guru. What gets shared as one is a painting, a modern actor in costume, or, more and more, an image made by a computer program in seconds. Second, the art. Sikh painting is old and much loved: scenes painted into janamsakhi manuscripts, portraits made in the Punjab hills and at Lahore, prints on the walls of countless homes. Many help people feel close to the Gurus, and there's nothing wrong with loving them. But each is an artist's picture, mostly made long after the Guru lived, and no one can be sure what any Guru looked like. Third, why it matters more here. Sikh teaching calls God nirankar, the formless, and the Guru now is the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. Pictures are not to be worshiped. So a painting can be treasured as a painting, without anyone claiming it's a likeness. Fourth, the habit. Sikhs themselves have been asking for more of it lately: check the date, ask who made it, and say painting when it's a painting. On this path, Guru Nanak kept asking gentle questions, like why throw water toward the sun? Asking isn't disrespect. That's today's line: a painting, not a photo.
screen: `THE GURUS: 1469 TO 1708.` · `CAMERAS: THE 1820S.` · `LOVED ART, NOT A LIKENESS.` · `CHECK, ASK, SAY PAINTING.` · then, large: `A PAINTING, NOT A PHOTO.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one picture. Bring to mind an image of a Guru you've seen, on a wall, a calendar, a phone. Hold it with affection. Breathe in, and let it give you what it gives: warmth, closeness, a face to turn toward. Breathe out, and say gently, inside: someone painted this, with love, long after. Notice that nothing is lost by saying it. The love stays. The facts settle into place. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Tasveer. A picture, a portrait. Every tasveer of a Guru is an artist's work, made long after; none is a photograph. Today's word.
Your line: a painting, not a photo. Love the art, and keep the facts straight. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: Paintings and prints of the Gurus hang in many Sikh homes and are loved as art; Sikh teaching holds that God is formless and that pictures are not to be worshiped, and no photograph of any Guru exists, since the Gurus lived from 1469 to 1708 and photography began in the 1820s.

match.prompt: dates and words — tap the pairs.

myth: there are real photographs of Guru Nanak
he died in 1539; photography began almost three centuries later.
Sikh art includes painted janamsakhi manuscripts and later portraits
loved by many, and mostly made long after the Gurus lived.
asking whether an image is real is disrespectful
Guru Nanak asked gentle questions all his life; checking is a kind of care.

fork.setup: a 'rare real photo' of a Guru is going round your family chat. what's the kind response?
options: forward it to everyone you know.
say gently that it's a painting or a made-up image, since cameras came much later.
reply that everyone in the chat is foolish.
fork.reveal: warm and true at once: the art can still be loved, and the caption can be fixed.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: tasveer, a picture or portrait; a word that came into Punjabi from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old photo of a Guru.
what it means: a painting, an actor, or a computer-made image; the Gurus lived long before cameras.
what a scholar hears: Sikh painting runs from illustrated janamsakhis through Pahari and Lahore portraits to modern prints; scholars debate whether any portrait was made in a Guru's lifetime.
recall: the Punjabi word for the turban

sources.ref: Nicéphore Niépce, View from the Window at Le Gras (c. 1826–27), the earliest surviving camera photograph
B. N. Goswamy, Piety and Splendour: Sikh Heritage in Art (National Museum, New Delhi, 2000)
Sikh Rehat Maryada, on Gurmat living (no idol or image worship; the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru)

Facts to confirm: the Gurus' dates (Guru Nanak born 1469; Guru Gobind Singh died 1708); the earliest surviving camera photograph (Niépce, c. 1826–27); that janamsakhi manuscripts were illustrated and that Pahari and Lahore portraits of the Gurus exist.
